By the end of this lecture, you will be able to…

items: 1Know why life is not possible on all planets — the atmospheric, thermal and water conditions that make a world habitable.
2Understand chemical and biological evolution — how simple molecules became complex organic molecules, and how those became self-sustaining, self-replicating systems.
3Explain the various ideas about the origin of life — special creation, panspermia, and spontaneous generation, and how each was supported or disproved.

blocks.x: Defining life
Life A process, feature or phenomenon capable of self-sustenance, replication and mutation.
Living system An open, self-organising thing that interacts with its environment, maintained by flows of information, energy and matter.
From simple molecules to a living cell
Simple molecules→ Vital monomers→ Polymerisation→ Biopolymer aggregation→ Protocell / membrane→ Reproductive machinery
Chemical evolution vs. biological evolution

c: The formation of complex organic molecules from simple molecules.
The formation of a self-sustaining, self-replicating system from complex organic molecules.

blocks.x: The lecture instructor is Seth Agyei Domfeh (MPhil, PGDTLHE, PhD), Department of Biochemistry and Biotechnology, KNUST.
Defining life & habitability
Life can be defined in several complementary ways, and living systems depend on very specific planetary conditions to arise and persist.
Life as signalling & self-sustaining processes

Life (2nd definition) A feature distinguishing physical entities having biological processes (signalling and self-sustaining processes) from those that do not, either because such functions have ceased or because they never had them (inanimate).
Life forms include animals, plants, protists, fungi, bacteria and archaea.
Organisms (3rd definition) Maintain homeostasis, are composed of cells, undergo metabolism, grow, adapt to their environment, respond to stimuli, and reproduce.
Living systems, Gaia & complex systems biology
Gaia hypothesis

Developed by James Lovelock: organisms interact with their inorganic surroundings to form a synergistic, self-regulating complex system that helps maintain and perpetuate the conditions for life on Earth — including global temperature, ocean salinity, atmospheric oxygen and the hydrosphere of liquid water.
Complex Systems Biology (CSB)

A branch of mathematical and theoretical biology concerned with the complexity of structure and function in organisms. CSB focuses on the emergence and evolution of organisms and species, and the complex interactions within bionetworks — with only partial overlap with complex systems theory and systems biology.
Habitability measures

Life does not occur on all planets because conditions on most planets do not support it. Conditions on Earth are right for the occurrence, sustenance and perpetuation of life — the presence of moisture, air and a suitable temperature is the proper condition for life.

blocks.title: Habitable Zone Distance (HZD) & Standard Primary Habitability (SPH)

items: HZD measures how far an exoplanet is from the centre of its star's habitable zone, in habitable zone units (HZU). Planets inside the habitable zone score between -1 and +1 HZU, with zero at the exact centre; negative/positive values correspond to locations closer/farther from the star. HZD is a function of the star's luminosity and temperature, and the planet's distance.

SPH measures the thermal-water climate suitability of a planet for land vegetation, on a scale of 0 to 1 (1 = most habitable). A mean surface temperature near 25°C (optimum for most vegetation) gives an SPH of 1; below -10°C or above 50°C is non-habitable. SPH is a function of surface temperature and relative humidity, though for exoplanets only the temperature component is calculated (water is assumed present).

Competing hypotheses
Three broad views have been proposed for the origination of life: special creation, colonisation (panspermia), and spontaneous generation.
View 1

Life is so complex that it requires a supernatural force to generate it — the Christian, Muslim and African traditionalist views. Critics say this view is mystical, cannot be proved, and does not obey natural laws. At least 10% of people in developed countries and 30% in developing countries believe in the supernatural origin of life and disease — a major obstacle to disease control.
View 2

Panspermia means "seeds everywhere." Life might have arisen from life forms elsewhere in the universe, arriving as living spores driven by light pressure or carried on rocks/meteorites. It espouses the extra-terrestrial origin of life and cannot be proved or refuted, since it only shifts the question of origin elsewhere.

items: Sales Gyon de Montlivant proposed life came from the moon.
H.E. Richter suggested life came from meteorites.
Svante Arrhenius proposed panspermia itself.
Francis Crick and Leslie Orgel proposed that intelligent forces may have directed the transport of life from elsewhere (directed panspermia).
About 7.5% of rocks ejected from Mars are estimated to reach Earth, taking between 100 and 16,000 years or more to arrive.

Evidence for panspermia: bacteria can survive the harsh environment of space (UV radiation, proton bombardment, cold) in a dormant state until awakened; meteorites contain amino acids (left-handed in helicity), bacteria and carbon protected inside rocks; Mars is arguably "safer" than early Earth — fewer bombardments, lower gravity, not as hot, and had oxygen when Earth did not.

blocks.x: Spontaneous generation (abiogenesis)

This theory asserts that life arose abiogenically. Aristotle (384–322 BC) suggested that when soil, straw or refuse free of life were left for a period, organisms could emerge from them freely if conditions were right — an idea supported by Van Velmont (1577–1644), John Needham (1713–1781) and Felix Pouchet (1859).
How spontaneous generation was disproved

1Redi, 1626–1697The "first blow": maggots grew on unsealed meat, none on sealed meat, only a few on gauze — never touching the meat itself. Disproved that maggots arise from decaying meat. 2Spallanzani, 1729–1799Boiling broth then sealing the flask immediately prevented microorganisms appearing; believers argued not enough oxygen remained. 31830sSchwann, Friedrich Schroder and von Dusch: air allowed in only after passing through a heated tube or sterile wool — no microbial growth resulted. 4Tyndall, 1820–1893Omission of dust → no growth. He demonstrated heat-resistant bacterial forms (endospores). 5Pasteur, 1822–1895His swan-neck flask trapped dust/microorganisms in the bend, keeping sterile liquid sterile indefinitely — unless tipped to let the trapped dust reach it. He ended the abiogenesis debate and is regarded as the father of Microbiology.

items: Rudolph Virchow (1858) reinforced the principle of biogenesis — life arises only from pre-existing life — building on Redi's earlier work.
The invention of the microscope by Anton van Leeuwenhoek in 1675 paved the way for studying the spontaneous generation of microbes, enabling later experiments like Spallanzani's and Pasteur's.

blocks.x: From simple molecules to biopolymers
In the 20th century, JBS Haldane and AL Oparin independently proposed that life evolved from non-living matter through a long-term process of chemical, then biological, evolution.
Long-term spontaneous generation

Raw materials for chemical evolution were readily available, together with suitable energy sources. The largest source of energy was sunlight; electrical discharges from lightning were another. Prebiotic synthesis drew primarily on the atmosphere, which contained hydrogen, methane, water vapour, ammonia and probably hydrogen sulphide, plus metallic sulphides and mineral phosphates from Earth's crust. Raw materials may also have been delivered by meteors and comets — carbonaceous meteorites contain organic molecules such as alcohols, aldehydes, amines, amino acids, purines and pyrimidines (and clays); comets are additional sources of carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen compounds.
The prebiotic (primordial) soup

Biologically vital compounds formed in the absence of oxygen in the atmosphere were spared any oxidative alteration. They persisted and were washed by rain into the oceans, building up in concentration to form the prebiotic/primordial soup — a pond or ocean where atmospheric chemicals plus an energy source combined to make amino acids, at least 4.5 billion years ago. Oparin and Haldane independently conceived this idea in 1920. It was once thought the first organisms were simple heterotrophs before mutating into autotrophs; evidence now suggests the first organisms were actually autotrophs.
The Miller–Urey experiment (1950)

Chemist Stanley Miller and physicist Harold Urey mixed gases thought present on primitive Earth — methane (CH₄), ammonia (NH₃), water (H₂O) and hydrogen (H₂), without oxygen — then electrically sparked the mixture to signify lightning. The result: amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.

blocks.x: Prebiotic synthesis of the four monomer classes

c: The formose reaction network — an excerpt starting from formaldehyde, proceeding through the Cannizzaro reaction, aldol reactions, isomerisation, β-elimination and 1,2-rearrangements to yield glycolaldehyde, glyceraldehyde, dihydroxyacetone, aldopentoses, aldohexoses and longer-chain sugars.
Strecker synthesis: ammonia reacts with an aldehyde to form an imine → cyanide (HCN) adds to the imine to form an aminonitrile → hydrolysis of the aminonitrile gives an amino acid.
Polymerisation of hydrogen cyanide (HCN) → diaminomaleonitrile → (with HCN, water, or other reagents) yields the purine bases adenine, hypoxanthine, xanthine and guanine.

Formic acid/oxalic acid → thermal decomposition → CO, H₂O, H₂, CO₂ → Fischer-Tropsch thermal processes → n-alkanes, n- and branched alkenes, n-alkanols (fatty alcohols), n-alkanoic acids (fatty acids), and n-alkyl formates (fatty formyl esters). High temperature and hydrogen pressure were required, though such conditions likely could not persist over an extended period in primitive times.

blocks.x: Polymerisation & condensing agents

Polymerisation Combining several monomers to form more complex molecules; through polymerisation, polysaccharides, polypeptides and polynucleotides could be formed. E.g. Glucose + Glucose ⇌ Disaccharide + H₂O — the forward reaction is a condensation reaction; the backward reaction is a hydrolytic reaction.

A condensation reaction is thermodynamically favoured if the water it forms is removed — by evaporation or by condensing agents. Condensing agents create a high-energy, more reactive intermediate, coupling the forward condensation reaction to their own uptake of the removed water.

Typically carry carbon linked by energetic double bonds to two nitrogens (-N=C=N-): carbodiimide (R-N=C=N-R), cyanogen (N≡C-C≡N), cyanamide (N≡CNH₂), diaminomaleonitrile, cyanoacetylene (N≡C-C≡CH), and polyphosphates such as ATP, whose free energy of hydration drives the reaction.

Dry heating (150–180°C) could polymerise monomers but risked decomposing the peptides formed over long exposure. Adsorption onto minerals — micas, clays (silicates attached to cations), and kaolin — concentrated pre-biological molecules and, via their positive/negative surface charges, acted as primitive catalytic centres.

blocks.title: Non-instructed vs. template-directed synthesis, and which came first: protein or nucleic acid?

items: Non-instructed synthesis of polypeptides/polynucleotides could occur by dry heating or by adding a condensing agent (e.g. a polyphosphate).
Template-directed synthesis of polypeptides falls into two categories: activated amino acids on a clay "template" (no sequence preference), or synthesis directed by a nucleic acid template.
Template-directed polynucleotide synthesis could use imidazole-activated monomers in the presence of divalent cations.

Proteins have structural/catalytic functions; nucleic acids are informational and can also act catalytically (e.g. ribozyme). The most plausible view is that proteins and nucleic acids evolved in parallel: polynucleotide replication coupled to polypeptide catalysis, with polynucleotides specifying polypeptides via translation, and polypeptides catalysing polynucleotide replication (and possibly translation).

blocks.x: From protocells to metabolism
The simplest structure that shows evidence of life is a cell — a compartment with a membrane separating it from its surroundings, so it is not diluted out of existence.
Coacervates, proteinoids & catalytic micelles
Oparin

Suggested the first cells emerged when a boundary or membrane formed around molecules with catalytic activity, most probably proteins. He called these 'cells' protobionts, formed through coacervation. Shortcoming: the coacervate droplets were formed from materials such as gum arabic, histone and albumin — substances living systems had already produced.
Fox

Fox's thermal proteinoids were micro-spheroidal aggregates; under suitable conditions they form microspheres that grow and eventually bud, with a two-layer membrane like that of bacteria. Problem: the membranes were too leaky.
Self-reproducing catalytic micelles as protocell precursors
Mixed micelle library→ Catalysed accretion→ Homeostatic growth→ Fission→ Compositional reproduction→ Vesicular protocell
Compositional mutations can arise during fission, feeding further evolution toward a vesicular protocell.
Development of metabolic pathways

Competition for nutrients in the cell led to the development of metabolic pathways. Evolved polymerisation reactions depended on the environment to supply monomeric units and energy-rich compounds such as ATP or polyphosphates. As essential components of the prebiotic soup became scarce, organisms developed enzymatic systems that could synthesise these substances from simpler but more abundant precursors — giving rise to energy-producing metabolic pathways that consumed other pre-existing energy-rich substances.

blocks.title: Why photosynthesis evolved, and the oxygen problem it created

items: As pre-existing energy-rich substances grew scarcer, the photosynthetic system evolved to exploit the sun, whose energy supply is inexhaustible.
Early photosynthesis used reducing agents such as H₂S, until this reductant was exhausted — driving refinement of the photosynthetic apparatus to use the ubiquitous reducing agent, H₂O.

Using water produced highly reactive O₂ as a by-product. To avoid oxidative damage from accumulating O₂, a much more efficient form of energy metabolism evolved that used the newly available O₂ as an oxidising agent.
